title: Positive-proportion pointwise lower bound: R(p) ≥ c·log²p for a positive proportion of primes (second-moment / Paley–Zygmund)
connection: From first and second moments of R(p) over p ≤ X, Paley–Zygmund gives R(p) ≥ ½E[R] on a positive proportion (F05w, F04).
why: A clean, likely provable intermediate theorem with the right order of magnitude — the 'Romanoff' rung of ES.
first_step: Check whether the second moment Σ_{p≤X} R(p)² ≪ X log⁴X is available (ET-type divisor-sum bounds) and write the Paley–Zygmund deduction.

title: Maynard–Tao multidimensional sieve over the (c,d) certificate grid
connection: Maynard–Tao weights (Σλ_{d1..dk})² detect many simultaneous 'prime/structured' events among k linear forms; the ES Type I certificate grid offers many linear-in-(c,d) objects at fixed p (e.g. moduli 4cd, values p²+4c²d).
why: MT weights produce 'at least m of k events happen' from first-moment data only — the shape we want for 'at least one certificate fires' — and here the average is over (c,d) at a single fixed p.
first_step: Write the k-tuple of events E_j = '4c_jd_j·(stuff) has a divisor ≡ −p mod 4c_jd_j' for an admissible family of (c_j,d_j) = (c0+jh, d0) and compute the MT ratio Σ_j S_j / S_0 numerically at p ~ 10^6.
refs: Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: Maynard 'Primes in APs to large moduli I–III' with p-dependent residue class
connection: Maynard (2020) extends Bombieri–Vinogradov-type results to moduli up to x^{3/5} for fixed residue classes and (part III) to uniform residue classes; ES needs divisors of p-tied integers in classes −p mod 4C that move with p.
why: Part III's uniformity in the residue class is exactly the feature a p-dependent class needs.
first_step: Read Maynard 'Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli III: uniform residue classes' and write the ES Type II count Σ_e #{ab | (p+e)/4 : a ≡ −b mod e} as a sum over moduli with residue a(p); identify which theorem shape is needed.
refs: Maynard, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli I, arXiv:2006.06572

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Tao higher uniformity in short intervals
connection: MRT (Annals 2023) prove Gowers/nilsequence uniformity of bounded multiplicative functions in almost all short intervals; ES counts are correlations of multiplicative-type indicator functions along affine forms in C.
why: Uniformity norms control linear-form correlations — e.g. Σ_C 1_{d | 4Cp+1}·1_{class}.
first_step: Write the C-average of the Type I indicator as a correlation of multiplicative functions along linear forms in C and identify which Gowers norm controls it.
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Tao–Teräväinen–Ziegler, Higher uniformity of bounded multiplicative functions in short intervals on average, arXiv:2007.15644

title: Green–Sawhney 'primes of the form p²+nq²' bilinear technique for p²+4c²d
connection: Green–Sawhney (2024) count primes of the form p² + nq² with p,q prime using Type I/II bilinear sieve on a binary quadratic form; ES Type I concerns divisors of p² + 4c²d, values of the same form shape.
why: Their Type II information on x² + n y² over thin variables is closely aligned with ES's quadratic value p² + 4c²d at fixed p.
first_step: Read Green–Sawhney's Type II estimate and check whether it gives equidistribution of divisors of p² + 4c²d in residue classes mod 4cd when c,d range over boxes at fixed p.
refs: Green–Sawhney, Primes of the form p^2 + nq^2, arXiv:2410.04189

title: Dunn–Kerr–Shparlinski–Zaharescu bilinear forms with modular square roots
connection: DKSZ bound bilinear sums Σ α_m β_n e(h√(mn)/q) over modular square roots; ES Type I at fixed f involves √(−4c²d) mod f, bilinear in (c, d).
why: Bilinear square-root sums are exactly what appears when one Fourier-expands the Type I condition in c and d.
first_step: Fourier-expand 1_{p² ≡ −4c²d (mod f)} and isolate the bilinear square-root sum; compare with DKSZ hypotheses.
refs: Dunn–Kerr–Shparlinski–Zaharescu, Bilinear forms in Weyl sums for modular square roots and applications, arXiv:1908.10143

title: Bettin–Chandee trilinear forms with Kloosterman fractions
connection: Bettin–Chandee bound Σ α_m β_n ν_a e(a·m̄/n); ES exponential sums carry e(h·\overline{4c}/p) or e(h·p̄/4c) fractions with three free variables (h, c, d).
why: Trilinear structure matches the three ES certificate parameters.
first_step: Write the Type I/II indicator's Fourier expansion, identify the trilinear Kloosterman-fraction sum, and check BC's ranges.
refs: Bettin–Chandee, Trilinear forms with Kloosterman fractions, arXiv:1502.00769

title: Polymath8 Type III / Deligne estimates for τ3-like ES counts
connection: Polymath8a's Type III estimates use Deligne's RH for correlations of hyper-Kloosterman sums to put τ3 in APs beyond 1/2; ES Type II solution counts are restricted triple-divisor counts (three denominators).
why: τ3-in-APs technology is the natural input for counting ES solutions in APs of n.
first_step: Write f(n) restricted to a fixed residue class of n as a τ3-type sum and test what level of distribution in n the ET average proof needs.
refs: Polymath, New equidistribution estimates of Zhang type, Algebra & Number Theory 8 (2014)

title: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard GCD-graph compression for the dependency structure across levels
connection: The Duffin–Schaeffer proof controls sets of integers with many pairs of large gcd by iterative 'GCD graph' compression. ES levels C are coupled through gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) | C′ − C. A GCD-graph style structure theorem might show that simultaneous failure of many levels forces a structured (compressible) configuration.
why: It is a modern combinatorial-analytic technique for exactly the 'many dependent arithmetic events' situation, and it has not obviously been tried.
first_step: Build the GCD graph on ES certificates at a hard prime (vertices = (C,d), edges weighted by gcd of the p-tied integers) and test KM's 'quality increment' lemma numerically.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0271] Read Koukoulopoulos–Maynard (Ann. Math. 2020) §§5–7; formulate the ES level-failure configuration as a weighted graph on levels with edge weights from shared primes.
[upgrades-0065] Over primes p ≤ 10⁸ estimate P(E_C ∩ E_C′)/(P(E_C)P(E_C′)) as a function of gcd(C,C′) and C/C′; fit a Duffin–Schaeffer-type overlap model.
refs: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard, On the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture (Ann. Math. 2020)
Koukoulopoulos–Maynard, On the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture, Ann. Math. 192 (2020), arXiv:1907.04593

title: Effective Duffin–Schaeffer (Koukoulopoulos–Maynard–Yang) quantitative overlap
connection: KMY give an effective version with explicit error terms; ES needs quantitative dependency bounds.
why: Quantitative control of overlaps among rational approximations is directly re-usable in second-moment ES arguments.
first_step: Read KMY's main quantitative lemma and extract its statement for sets of moduli of the form 4Cp+1 divisors.
refs: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard–Yang, An almost sharp quantitative version of the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture, arXiv:2404.14628

title: Petrow–Young Weyl bound for Dirichlet L-functions and character sums mod 4C
connection: Petrow–Young (Annals 2020) prove the Weyl-strength subconvex bound L(1/2,χ) ≪ q^{1/6+ε} for all Dirichlet χ; ES counts expand over characters mod 4C.
why: Subconvexity controls the character-sum error terms in Type I/II counts at fixed C.
first_step: Write the ES count at fixed (p,C) via Σ_χ mod 4C and determine whether subconvexity in q = 4C (small) or in the p-aspect is the bottleneck.
refs: Petrow–Young, The Weyl bound for Dirichlet L-functions of cube-free conductor, Ann. Math. 192 (2020), arXiv:1811.02452

title: Thorner–Zaman effective Chebotarev for least prime with prescribed Frobenius
connection: Thorner–Zaman give unconditional bounds for the least prime in a Chebotarev class ≪ D^{c}; ES forcing lines (F_q: '(q/p) = −1 ⇒ ES(p)') need a small prime with prescribed splitting.
why: Quantifies how far unconditional least-prime technology is from what a fixed-q forcing line needs.
first_step: List, for each ES forcing lemma in EXSET_CHAR_FORCING.md, the Chebotarev class needed and plug Thorner–Zaman's exponent.
refs: Thorner–Zaman, An explicit bound for the least prime ideal in the Chebotarev density theorem, Algebra & Number Theory 11 (2017), arXiv:1604.01750

title: Explicit Burgess (Treviño) for the least non-residue ES forcing line
connection: Treviño's explicit Burgess bounds give explicit n₂(p) ≪ p^{1/(4√e)}-type constants; ES is classically settled when the least QNR is 3, 5 or 7 — the F_q line.
why: Makes the 'generic point of the least-QNR line' quantitative and checkable against 10^18 verification.
first_step: Compute, with explicit Burgess, how large p must be before n₂(p) ≤ 13 can fail and record it alongside the ES verification bound.
refs: Treviño, The least k-th power non-residue, J. Number Theory 149 (2015)

title: Platt–Trudgian / explicit zero-free regions for explicit exceptional-set constants
connection: Recent explicit zero-free regions and RH verification to large heights (Platt–Trudgian 2021) feed explicit prime-counting in APs; the repo's exceptional-set bounds are ineffective-constant.
why: Explicit E(N) bounds combined with verification could say 'no counterexample below X with a given property' — calibration, not a proof.
first_step: List which steps of the 3/4-exponent note use Siegel–Walfisz and replace by explicit Bennett–Martin–O'Bryant–Rechnitzer estimates.
refs: Platt–Trudgian, The Riemann hypothesis is true up to 3·10^12, Bull. LMS 53 (2021)
Bennett–Martin–O'Bryant–Rechnitzer, Explicit bounds for primes in arithmetic progressions, Illinois J. Math. 62 (2018)

title: OAI 003 zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8 (claimed) as an unconditional GRH-substitute
connection: The local OAI dump claims all Dirichlet L-functions are zero-free for Re s > 7/8; the repo's GRH-conditional ES statements (least-QNR, M_gen lower bounds) could become unconditional with fixed-strip exponents.

title: OAI 'uniform exclusion of Landau–Siegel zeros' (claimed) → effective ternary-form theorems
connection: The OAI dump claims (1−β) log q ≥ c for all real zeros; ineffective ES-adjacent theorems (Siegel-based class number lower bounds, Duke–Schulze-Pillot ternary representations) would become effective.

title: Xylouris / Linnik constant L ≤ 5 for least prime ≡ −p mod 4C
connection: Linnik's theorem with L = 5 bounds the least prime in an AP mod q by q^5; ES Type II with a prime denominator needs primes in classes tied to p.
why: Shows how far uniform AP results are from what is needed; calibration of the B2 gap.

refs: Xylouris, Über die Nullstellen der Dirichletschen L-Funktionen und die kleinste Primzahl in einer arithmetischen Progression (2011)

title: Leng–Sah–Sawhney quasipolynomial inverse theorem for Gowers norms
connection: LSS give quasi-polynomial bounds in the U^k inverse theorem and Szemerédi; linear-form correlations of ES indicators are controlled by Gowers norms.
why: Quantitative inverse theorems are needed for any averaged ES correlation estimate with power-of-log savings.
first_step: Identify the Gowers norm controlling the ET average Σ_{p≤x} f(p) along linear forms in (c,d,e) and estimate the loss with LSS bounds.
refs: Leng–Sah–Sawhney, Improved bounds for Szemerédi's theorem, arXiv:2402.17995

title: Strömbergsson–Venkatesh small solutions to linear congruences
connection: Strömbergsson–Venkatesh study the distribution of the smallest solution of linear congruences via equidistribution of lattices; ES certificates are small solutions of congruences with modulus tied to p.
why: Gives the limiting distribution of 'smallest certificate size', comparable with ES's forced windows.
first_step: Write the ES Type II certificate as a small solution of a linear congruence system mod 4cd and compare its size distribution with SV's limit law.
refs: Strömbergsson–Venkatesh, Small solutions to linear congruences and Hecke equidistribution, Acta Arith. 118 (2005)

title: OAI 007 ordinary two-point Chowla (claimed) for λ-weighted ES counts
connection: OAI 007 claims Σ_{n≤X} λ(a₁n+b₁)λ(a₂n+b₂) ≪ X/(log X)^c for fixed affine forms; ES certificate counts can be twisted by λ of the p-tied integers to detect parity structure.
why: Parity of Ω(4Cp+1) correlates with whether its divisors can split into classes; ordinary (non-log) two-point Chowla removes the log-averaging that blocked earlier transfers.
first_step: Check whether 'number of divisors ≡ −1 (mod 4) of N' correlates with λ(N) for N in an AP, and if so formulate the needed correlation along the forms (4Cp+1, 4C′p+1).

title: Smooth numbers in all short intervals (Matomäki–Radziwiłł; Teräväinen) → smooth slice existence
connection: MR prove every interval [x, x + C√x] contains x^ε-smooth numbers? (check exact statement); a smooth slice N_e has many small prime factors and likely succeeds.
why: An 'every interval' smooth-number theorem is a pointwise tool; the slice window near p/4 is short (polylog?) so the needed length must be compared.
first_step: Check the exact current record for smooth numbers in every short interval and compare with the number of slices available at p (e < some bound).
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł, Multiplicative functions in short intervals, Ann. Math. 183 (2016), §1 (smooth numbers in short intervals)

title: Vinogradov's least-QNR conjecture as a sufficient hypothesis for the BM layer only
connection: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9: the BM layer is pointwise free, i.e. some level 4 | t ≤ 4ℓ(p) has a positive main term. The remaining question is the class of the divisor inside a coset. Least-QNR bounds control the first layer only.
why: This calibrates what 'standard conjectures' buy; the second layer needs a different hypothesis (equidistribution of divisor classes of one integer).
first_step: Formulate the minimal second-layer hypothesis ('divisors of tp+1 equidistribute in (ℤ/t)^× for some t ≤ T') and compare it with the known Erdős–Hall/Montgomery-type results on divisor class distribution.

title: Kloosterman-sum form of the word count R_t(p) and Weil-bound positivity
connection: #{(X,Y): XY = tp+1, X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (t), sizes} is a divisor-in-progression count. Its sign-twisted version Σ(A/p) is a sum of Jacobi symbols over divisors, expressible by Kloosterman/Salié sums after Poisson summation.
why: Weil's bound is the native positivity tool. It needs long sums, and the word count per level is O(1), which is the B3 issue in native terms.
first_step: Write the χ-twisted level-t count as a Salié sum expression and record the length vs modulus ratio.

title: Height zeta function of the threefold 𝒰 and its analytic continuation
connection: Σ_{(n,x,y,z) ∈ 𝒰(ℤ_{>0})} H(n,x,y,z)^{−s} counts all ES solutions. Its rightmost pole gives the log²-order average count (ET). Its analytic structure, e.g. as a sum of Eisenstein-type series via the torsor, is native to Manin-conjecture methods (Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel).
why: Analytic continuation gives secondary terms, which control the lower tail in short intervals of n, a step towards almost-all-with-rates.
first_step: Write the height zeta function via ET's parametrisation as a multiple Dirichlet series and identify its polar structure.
refs: Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel, Igusa integrals and volume asymptotics (2010)

title: Pretentious multiplicative functions: forest monochromaticity forces χ_p to 'pretend' to be 1
connection: If ES₅ fails, χ_p(u) = χ_p(v) on all forest edges (forest form). For a completely multiplicative ±1 function this is a strong constraint along a sparse set of multiplicative relations. Granville–Soundararajan pretentiousness quantifies when f behaves like 1 on structured sets.
why: Halász-type theorems give strong conclusions from pretentiousness. If edge constraints imply Σ_{q ≤ X}(1 − χ_p(q))/q small, this would contradict known lower bounds for the least QNR's 'pretentious distance' (or not).
first_step: Translate the edge constraints χ(u)χ(v) = 1 into constraints on χ at primes for small u, v; compute the implied D(χ_p, 1; X) bound and compare with Burgess-type lower bounds.
refs: Granville–Soundararajan, Pretentious multiplicative functions and an inequality for the zeta-function (2008)

title: Explicit Burgess (Treviño) to make the 'BM layer is pointwise free' statement fully explicit
connection: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9 Prop 2.2: some 4 | t ≤ 4ℓ(p) has a positive BM main term iff p is not a square. Explicit Burgess bounds (Treviño, McGown) give explicit ℓ(p) ≤ p^{1/4√e+ε}-type bounds with constants.
why: It gives an explicit, verifiable statement that is the first layer of ES, for formal verification and for any explicit-range argument.
first_step: Plug Treviño's explicit least-QNR bound into Prop 2.2; state the explicit level bound for all p ≥ 10²⁰.
refs: Treviño, The least quadratic non-residue and related problems (2015; check)

title: Explicit Burgess constants (Treviño-type) for the Legendre-sum T(p) in M_BM
connection: Helfgott needed fully explicit major arcs; the ES analogue is an explicit version of Thm 2.2 (M_BM(p) ≥ (3/16π² − o(1)) log²p), whose o(1) comes from Burgess on Σ(−m/p)w(m).
why: An explicit M_BM ≥ c·log²p for all p ≥ p₁ is a prerequisite of every H⁻_BM-type route and is purely a bookkeeping task with existing explicit Burgess inequalities.
first_step: Treviño, 'The Burgess inequality and the least kth power non-residue', IJNT 11 (2015) 1653–1678, arXiv:1412.3062 gives explicit Burgess estimates (verified, data/z52b/upgrades_leads_check.md); check that its ranges cover the weighted hyperbolic sum T(p) and compute the resulting explicit p₁.

title: Vinogradov bilinear decomposition of the (★) count
connection: Vinogradov's Type I/II bilinear sums made ternary Goldbach unconditional. R(p) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cp+1 : d ≡ −1 (4C)} is a sum over factorizations ab = 4Cp+1; split by the sizes of a, b, C into 'Type I' (one factor short: congruence sums in C) and 'Type II' (both medium: bilinear forms in (a,b)).
why: Gives a structured place where cancellation must be found; the Type I part may be treatable pointwise in p by elementary counting.
first_step: Write R(p) = Σ_{a,b} α_a β_b 1[ab ≡ 1 mod 4C, ab = 4Cp+1] with dyadic ranges; compute numerically which range carries the solutions for p ~ 10⁸–10¹⁰.

title: An ineffective 'all large p' theorem is acceptable progress
connection: DSP (via Siegel) is ineffective yet counted as a full upgrade. For ES, an ineffective theorem 'ES(p) for p > p₀ (ineffective)' would already be a first-ever all-large result.
why: Opens Siegel-type inputs (L(1,χ) ≫ q^{−ε}) that the campaign may have discarded because they are ineffective.

title: Linnik's three principles for the least ES certificate
connection: Linnik made Dirichlet effective-for-every-q with: log-free zero density, zero-free region, Deuring–Heilbronn repulsion. ES analogue: bound the least level C(p) (or least e) carrying a certificate by p^L, organising the proof as (a) 'density' of bad character configurations, (b) a 'zero-free' range for small moduli, (c) an exceptional character making other families easier.
why: Every bound C(p) < ∞ already is ES, so the content is the three-part architecture: separating 'few bad characters' from 'one exceptional character'.
first_step: Write the BM-level positivity proof (least ℓ with (p/ℓ) = −1) as principle (b), and formulate precisely what principle (a) would have to say about order-≥3 characters mod 4C.

title: Intermediate milestone: (★)-primes in every short interval
connection: Every interval [x, x + x^{0.525}] contains primes (BHP) and the ES exceptional set in short intervals satisfies E(I) ≪ H exp(−c(log H)^{3/4}) ((D)30), so every such interval contains primes satisfying the sub-route — check that this holds for (★) itself and for Mordell-hard classes.
why: A cheap, honest 'every interval' theorem; it calibrates which short-interval statements are already free and which are not (e.g. intervals of length (log x)^A).
first_step: Verify that the short-interval exceptional-set bound applies to (★) restricted to p ≡ 1 (mod 840) and combine with BHP for primes in progressions to get the statement; then ask for the shortest H where it holds.

title: Heilbronn case split: ES under GRH-type regularity, and ES under its failure
connection: Heilbronn proved h(−d) → ∞ by: if GRH holds, Hecke; if it fails, the false zero itself forces the result. ES: prove (a) ES for all large p assuming a regularity hypothesis R on the characters (·/p), (·/ℓ) and (b) ES for all large p assuming ¬R (some exceptional character), with (b) using the exceptional bias.
why: Each half is conditional, the union unconditional — a proven almost→every template that tolerates ignorance about which case holds.
first_step: Formulate R as the minimal statement H⁻_BM needs (BM_CORRECTED §3.3 says no standard conjecture implies it — find the weakest one that does), then analyse what ¬R gives for the window/b=1 families.

title: Maynard multidimensional weights over an auxiliary parameter
connection: Maynard: with k linear forms, sieve weights force at least m of them prime. For fixed p, take k candidate certificate families indexed by an auxiliary integer t (e.g. windows q(t) in progressions) and use multidimensional weights to force at least one success.
why: Converts 'one family must succeed' into a sieve-weight positivity problem over t, where averaging is legitimate (t is free, p fixed).
first_step: Identify a free auxiliary variable t such that each family's success at t is a 'primality-like' event of a polynomial in t; write the GPY/Maynard ratio for the toy model.

title: Geometric cancellation via trace functions for divisor-class sums
connection: Deligne's Ramanujan bound comes from geometry (purity). The ES deviation involves sums over characters of order ≥ 3 mod 4C of σ_χ(4Cp+1); for prime moduli these are sums of trace functions (Kummer sheaves) where Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel give square-root cancellation in long sums.
why: If the ES non-genus part X(p) can be written as a sum of trace functions with conductor bounded independently of p, Deligne-type bounds apply pointwise.
first_step: Restrict to prime levels 4C → prime e (windows) and write the e-slice certificate count as a trace-function sum over divisors; compute the conductors.

title: Lower bound by upper bounds on complements (Stepanov/Weil principle)
connection: In the elementary proofs of Weil's bound, the lower bound for N comes from upper bounds applied to complementary objects. ES: find a family {R_j(p)} with R_0 = R(p) whose total Σ_j R_j(p) has a pointwise asymptotic and whose other members have sharp pointwise upper bounds; then R(p) ≥ total − Σ_{j≠0} upper bounds.
why: Upper bounds for divisor counts in fixed classes (Shiu/Brun–Titchmarsh type) are much easier than lower bounds; the total over all classes (τ(4Cp+1) summed over C) has a known asymptotic.
first_step: Quantify at small levels (C ≤ 8, where φ(4C) ≤ 16): total τ-sum asymptotic vs. best upper bounds for each wrong class; how sharp must the upper bounds be for R(p) > 0 to follow?

title: Fourier reduction of an ES obstruction to a multiplicative (character) obstruction
connection: Tao reduced EDP to completely multiplicative functions by Fourier analysis. ES failure at window e means no divisor ratio ≡ −1 (mod e); reduce this to the existence of a character (or approximate homomorphism) χ mod e with χ(−1) = −1 that is 'large' on the prime factors of N_e.
why: If every obstruction is character-like, the problem becomes one about Legendre/higher-order characters at p — the BM/genus language where tools exist.
first_step: Prove the reduction for prime e: if the ±1-subset products of {g_i} miss −1, is there a character χ with χ(−1) = −1 and Σ_i Re χ(g_i) large? Test on data.

title: Almost-all + one more set ⇒ all: ES with a third free 'rescue' parameter
connection: In Gowers's trick, AB covers all but few elements and a third factor rescues the rest. ES: (★) covers all but a thin set of p (the 14 failures ≤ 10¹⁰); b=1 covers all but 3; their union none ≤ 10⁸. Formalise a 'rescue family' whose success set is large in a way that must intersect any thin exceptional set of the first family.
why: Converts the empirical complementarity of routes into a cardinality argument (needs a lower bound on the rescue family's success set within every thin structured set).
first_step: Characterise the (★)-exceptional set structurally (residue conditions, ℓ(p)) and compute the b=1 success rate restricted to primes with that structure.

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł-type short-interval averages of R(n): what is free and what is not
connection: MR show multiplicative functions behave in almost all short intervals of length h → ∞; every-interval statements need h ≥ x^θ. For ES: the average of R(n) over almost all intervals of length (log n)^A is ≈ M; the step to every interval mirrors the step to every n.
why: Clarifies the ladder: every n ⇐ every short interval of length 1; quantify the shortest interval length for which an every-interval result can be proved.
first_step: Combine the short-interval exceptional-set bound (D)30 with the primes-in-short-intervals literature to find the smallest H(x) such that every [x, x+H] contains a prime with a (★) certificate.
refs: arXiv:1501.04585 (Matomaki-Radziwill, Multiplicative functions in short intervals)

title: Dimension-zero exceptional set as an intermediate target
connection: Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss showed Littlewood's exceptional set has Hausdorff dimension 0 via measure rigidity. ES analogue: E(N) ≪ N^ε (zero 'dimension') — strictly between the current N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) and finiteness.
why: A measure-rigidity or entropy approach might reach 'dimension 0' even if CRT sieves stop at exponent 3/4 (EXCEPTIONAL_KARY3).
first_step: Formulate the profinite/adelic dynamical system whose invariant measures would control ES exceptions and check whether an entropy argument bounds the counting dimension of the exceptional set.

title: Real-variable circle method for 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/p
connection: Count near-solutions via ∫ S(α)³ e(−4α/p) K(α) dα with S(α) = Σ_{x≤X} e(α/x) (van der Corput sums of smooth phases); exact solutions need tolerance ~ 1/(pxyz), far below what such integrals resolve.
why: Not nonsense: it gives the density of near-solutions and the scale at which arithmetic must take over; it locates the 'resolution gap' quantitatively.
first_step: Estimate the number of triples with |1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 4/p| < δ as a function of δ via the integral and compare with exact counts for p ≤ 10⁵.

title: τ₃ in progressions beyond 1/2 (Type III / Kloosterman–Deligne) for the shifted-d₃ reading
connection: Zhang/Polymath used Type III estimates: the ternary divisor function in APs to moduli beyond √x via Deligne's bounds (Friedlander–Iwaniec, Heath-Brown, Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel). ES words count (u,B,C) with 4uBC = p + u + B — a shifted d₃-type count; METAPLECTIC notes a shifted-d₃/GL(3)-Eisenstein reading.
why: If ES can be put as 'τ₃-like function of a shifted argument in a progression', Type III technology offers power savings in exactly the needed shape.
first_step: Write the (u, B, C) count as Σ_{n} τ₃-like(n) over n in a progression determined by p; identify the modulus size relative to the length.

title: Goldfeld–Gross–Zagier-type effectivity: an auxiliary L-function with a high-order zero
connection: Goldfeld showed that an L-function with a zero of order ≥ 3 at s = 1/2 makes Siegel effective (Gross–Zagier supplied it). For an ineffective ES theorem (via Siegel), an analogous auxiliary object with a forced high-order vanishing would make p₀ explicit.
why: Only relevant once an ineffective all-large-p ES theorem exists, but it shows the route from ineffective to effective is not blocked in principle.
first_step: List places where Siegel's theorem could enter an ES argument (main-term lower bounds via L(1,χ)) and check whether Goldfeld's effective bound (h(−d) ≫ log d) is enough there.

title: Logarithmic density as an intermediate notion for ES-type sub-routes
connection: Tao's Collatz and Chowla results hold in logarithmic density, which is easier than natural density. For ES sub-routes whose failure sets might be infinite (e.g. (★) alone), compute logarithmic-density statements and the corresponding 'log-averaged' tools (Tao's entropy decrement).
why: Log-averaging made several almost-all results possible where natural density was stuck; useful for sub-route exceptional sets.
first_step: Estimate Σ_{p ≤ X, (★) fails} 1/p numerically and check whether log-averaged tools give a finite bound.
refs: arXiv:1909.03562 (Tao, Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values)

title: Ineffective all-large p for the subfamily of p with a bounded non-residue profile
connection: Duke–Schulze-Pillot's theorem is ineffective but for every large n. Target: 'for every fixed L, all sufficiently large p with ℓ(p) ≤ L satisfy ES' (ineffectively). Since ℓ(p) ≤ L for 100% of primes as L → ∞, this would be a strong almost-all-with-structure result.
why: Combines the guaranteed BM positivity at small ℓ with a Siegel-type ineffective control of the error at those levels.
first_step: Formulate the restricted count using only levels built from primes ≤ L and estimate its main term vs error for fixed L as p → ∞.

title: GRH + computation template for ES sub-routes with explicit exceptions
connection: Ono–Soundararajan: GRH-conditional explicit threshold + computation to 2·10¹⁰ gives an exact exception list. For a sub-route whose failures are explicitly known (b=1 line: 193, 2521, 66529 ≤ 10¹¹), attempt a GRH-conditional proof that there are no further failures.
why: A conditional complete classification for a sub-route would be a first 'every p' theorem (conditional) in the ES landscape.
first_step: Identify the sub-route with the simplest certificate condition (b=1: p + 4d has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4d) and attempt a GRH-conditional lower bound for its count with explicit constants.

title: Saving in x versus saving in H: the exact form an every-n exceptional bound must take
connection: Every-interval results for primes need savings depending on the location x, not only on the interval length H. For ES, (D)30 gives E(I) ≪ H exp(−c(log H)^{3/4}); a bound E(I) ≪ H·exp(−c(log x)^θ) uniform down to H = 1 would be < 1 for H ≤ exp(c(log x)^θ), hence ES. So the target is an x-dependent saving in short intervals.
why: Makes precise how 'almost all in short intervals' must improve to reach 'every': any argument giving savings in log x at fixed small H is already pointwise.
first_step: Re-examine the (D)30 proof and identify where the saving is tied to H (the number of n averaged) rather than to x; ask whether any piece gives x-dependent savings.

title: Prime-capture problems: every prime is caught by an infinite family of Chebotarev conditions
connection: A finite family of congruence conditions catches every large prime only if it contains all coprime classes modulo some M (Dirichlet), and finite families of splitting conditions can catch all primes only in special configurations (e.g. ℚ(√2), ℚ(√3), ℚ(√6) — reviewer example); bounded-modulus ES congruence families provably miss the square classes; ES Type II (abelian conditions p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB) and Type I (dihedral conditions via ring class fields) are infinite families with conductors up to ≍ p. List known 'every prime is captured by a family with conductor ≤ f(p)' theorems (e.g. least non-residue: some ℓ ≤ p^{0.152} has (p/ℓ) = −1) and place ES among them.
why: Identifies the closest proven 'prime-capture' statements and how their conductor bounds compare with what ES needs.
first_step: Write the conductor/size of the capturing family for ES sub-routes and for known capture theorems (Burgess, Linnik, Vinogradov) in one table.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x^2 + ny^2 (1989)

title: Exceptional set of the two-term step is tiny: 'almost all two-term + rescue' structure
connection: Goldbach–Linnik used that the binary Goldbach exceptional set is small enough for a sparse rescue set. In ES, the two-term step m/N = 1/y + 1/z (after choosing x) fails on a thin set of (m, N); show that for every p, among the ≍ p choices of x the pairs (m_x, N_x) cannot all lie in that thin set, using its explicit structure.
why: The thin exceptional set of the two-term problem is explicit (divisor-class avoidance), so 'cannot all avoid' is a concrete combinatorial statement.
first_step: Characterise {(m, N) : m/N not a sum of two unit fractions} for small m and compute the fraction of x ∈ (p/4, p/2) for which (4x − p, px) lands in it, for hard p.

title: Which almost-all ES results are sharp in the Kolmogorov sense?
connection: Kolmogorov's divergent Fourier series shows some a.e. theorems are optimal. For each ES-type almost-all theorem (single levels, (★), b=1, ES₅), decide whether infinitely many failures are known/expected (then the almost-all result is 'sharp') or not; only the latter are candidates for every-p upgrades.
why: Avoids attempting upgrades of statements that are actually false infinitely often (like single-level or (★)-only versions may be).
first_step: For each sub-route, estimate Σ_p P(fail) under the calibrated model; classify as 'expected finitely many' vs 'expected infinitely many' failures.
refs: Kolmogorov, Fund. Math. 4 (1923)/ C. R. 1926 (everywhere divergent L^1 Fourier series)

title: Finite-field point count of the cleared ES surface is n-independent: q² + 1 affine points
connection: For odd q and n ≢ 0, the affine surface 4xyz = n(xy + yz + zx) over F_q has exactly q² + 1 points (checked for q = 5, 7, 11 and n = 1, 2, 3; for n ≡ 0 it is 3q² − 3q + 1). So the local factor at primes ℓ ∤ 2n carries no arithmetic of n; n enters the singular series only at ℓ | 2n and through the integrality/positivity of reciprocals.
why: Removes a candidate source of 'hard prime' structure: small-prime local densities cannot distinguish hard from easy p; the distinction must come from the p-adic factor, the archimedean window, or global effects.
first_step: Derive the expected count of Type I/II solutions including the quadratic-character term from the Brauer element and compare its predicted per-prime weights with the fitted β_q ≈ −0.35/q.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0320] Prove the q² + 1 count (fibre over each (y, z) is a point unless 4yz = n(y + z) and nyz = 0); then compute the p-adic density at ℓ = p exactly.
[analogues-0042] Compute refined local densities (solutions with prescribed valuations / unit patterns) at ℓ ≤ 50 and at ℓ = p; check for any n-dependence via Legendre symbols.

title: Norm descent: multiply an O_K solution by its conjugate
connection: From 4/n = Σ1/x_i and 4/n = Σ 1/x_i' (conjugates), the product (Σ1/x_i)(Σ1/x_i') = 16/n² gives 16/n² as a 9-term sum of 1/(x_i x_j'); pairing diagonal terms 1/N(x_i) gives integer unit fractions.
why: Exhibits a route from a proved world to a k-term integer Egyptian representation of 16/n²; probably weaker than ES but a concrete transfer statement.
first_step: Write the 9 terms and check when the off-diagonal pairs x_i x_j' + x_j x_i' combine into integers; test with the D = 2 identity.

title: Weil restriction view: ES over O_K for rational n = system of ES-like equations over Z in [K:Q] variables
connection: Writing x_i = a_i + b_i√D turns the O_K equation into two integer equations (rational and irrational parts) in six variables. Prop 3.3 solutions give an explicit family of integer points on this 6-variable variety.
why: The 6-variable integer variety contains the ES surface (b_i = 0); proved points on it might deform (via an integral curve) toward b_i = 0.
first_step: Write the two equations, then look for curves through the Prop 3.3 points meeting the b = 0 locus.

title: Sums of three cubes (Booker–Sutherland): cubic surfaces with integral points, heuristics vs truth
connection: x³ + y³ + z³ = k is a cubic surface with a local obstruction (k ≡ ±4 mod 9) and Heath-Brown's heuristic predicts infinitely many solutions otherwise; ES is a cubic surface too, with no local obstruction and polylog expected count at fixed n.
why: The three-cubes world shows that 'heuristically infinitely many' and 'every k has one' are proved only by search; ES at fixed p is the same type of question with much smaller search spaces.
first_step: Compare expected-count heuristics: Heath-Brown's for three cubes vs log²p for ES; note no proof technique exists in either world for pointwise existence.

title: Elliptic-curve world: fixing one denominator ratio gives a curve; ES ⇔ integral point on some curve in a pencil
connection: Setting y = t·x (rational t) turns ES into a conic/curve in (x, z); a pencil of curves over t covers the ES surface. Each curve's integral points are governed by its genus (0 here), so ES ⇔ some member of a pencil of conics has an integral point.
why: Pencils of conics with integral points: a Hasse-principle-for-integral-points question per member; Mordell's divisor approach is this in disguise.

connection: Hasse principle for diagonal cubic surfaces (Swinnerton-Dyer; Heath-Brown–Skorobogatov) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: —. Obstruction: BM. Status: conditional (finiteness of Sha / Schinzel's H). Mechanism: fibration method + descent.

connection: Harpaz studies integral points on log K3 surfaces (complements of anticanonical boundaries) with a fibration in conics, computing Brauer groups and proving HP/strong approximation under Schinzel; U_n fibres over the x-line in hyperbola-type curves ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = n²x².

connection: For fixed n the ES equation defines an affine cubic surface; integral-point counting conjectures (Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel; Wilsch, Santens for log Fano) predict (log H)^b growth with a product of local densities as constant.
why: Gives a principled 'singular series' for R(n): ES fails only if the leading constant vanishes (T1?) or by fluctuation.

title: minz(p) is always a multiple of p (p ≤ 2·10⁵)
connection: For every prime p ≤ 2·10⁵ the least possible largest denominator minz(p) ≡ 0 (mod p) (OEIS-style constant-zero transform).
why: If provable it pins the optimal solution's structure: the largest denominator always carries p; could give an extremal-solution parametrisation and a minimal-height bound.
first_step: Try to prove: in any solution of 4/p with largest denominator z, if p ∤ z then z ≥ … > some solution with p | z; else find a counterexample for composite-free p beyond 2·10⁵.

title: U(p) vs smoothness of p−1: ρ(P⁺(p−1) exponent) = +0.40
connection: log P⁺(p−1)/log p correlates +0.40 with U(p) residual: smooth p−1 ⇒ hard.
why: Smooth shifted primes have positive density for P⁺(p−1) ≤ p^{0.2961} (Baker–Harman, cited in FORCED_WINDOW.md); ES-hard primes may be concentrated there, which is a thin set amenable to separate treatment.
first_step: Estimate density of 'ES-hard' (ratio below 0.3) among primes with P⁺(p−1) ≤ p^{1/3} vs others.

title: For p ≡ 3 (mod 4) the weights are a clean positive Euler product in χ_{−p}
why: At p ≡ 3 (4) ES is trivial, yet the count law is a textbook Euler product — ES counts are governed by the local densities of the surface; the p ≡ 1 (4) case is the same law with sign flip and shift confounds.
first_step: Derive the local density at q of solutions of 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z (Elsholtz–Tao §2-style) as a function of (q/p) and compare to q·β_q ≈ 0.4.

title: Toric ideals of monomial substitutions
connection: Encode multiplicative relations among denominator components as binomial equations and study their toric moves.
why: Toric structure may organize equivalent factorizations without confusing them with the additive ES condition.
first_step: For one gcd parametrization, list its monomial map and derive elementary binomial relations.

title: Degree profiles versus denominator heights
connection: Classify polynomial certificates by the three denominator degrees and compare them with logarithmic integer heights.
why: Degree balance can expose cancellation regimes that are difficult to see in numerical size data.
first_step: Enumerate degree profiles in a small odd-characteristic model and derive the leading-coefficient cancellation conditions.

title: Fibrations with arithmetic sections
connection: View a chosen auxiliary parameter as the base of a fibration and look for sections that are integral on specified congruence classes.
why: A section supplies a family; its arithmetic domain can be analyzed independently of generic rational solvability.
first_step: For a simple conic fibration, find one rational section and derive its integer-specialization conditions.

title: Torsor coordinates for gcd removal
connection: Introduce auxiliary variables to encode pairwise coprimality and factor allocation, seeking a torsor-like parametrization.
why: Such coordinates may separate multiplicative structure from the main additive equation.

title: Determinant-method maps of certificate concentration
connection: Use low-degree polynomial relations to describe where bounded certificates cluster on the surface.
why: A concentration theorem or experiment could suggest missing parametrizations rather than serve as a reason to discard a route.
first_step: Fit low-degree curves to a bounded set of exact points and check containment symbolically before consulting determinant-method estimates.

title: Painlevé VI and cubic surfaces: U_n as a character variety
connection: Cubic surfaces xyz + x² + y² + z² + ax + by + cz + d = 0 (Fricke/character varieties) carry Painlevé VI dynamics and nonlinear monodromy. Check whether U_n (4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)) is birational to such a Fricke cubic.
why: Fricke cubics have infinite integral automorphism groups (Markoff-type); if U_n is one, the orbit structure of integer points is the whole story.
first_step: Attempt the explicit birational map: put x = n·X etc. and complete to a Fricke normal form; or run Sage to compute the Picard lattice and (−2)-curves of the projective closure of U_n (repo already knows its singularities? git grep 'Fricke').

title: Compare ES with x/y + y/z + z/x = n (Bremner–Guy): both are 'n as a value of a symmetric rational function in 3 variables'; the latter reduces to elliptic curves with rank-dependent solvability — what makes ES's function (harmonic mean) different?
connection: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z says n/4 is... the harmonic mean of x,y,z divided by 3: HM/3·… ; x/y + y/z + z/x = n defines a cubic curve in P² for each n (genus 1); 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is a cubic surface (dimension 2) — more freedom, hence many solutions (log²n) rather than rank-controlled finitely many. So ES is 'easier' in count but lacks the group law. A middle ground: intersect U_n with a plane (e.g. z = x + y or z = kx) to get a curve; integer points on these curves (genus 0 or 1) — for genus 0 fibres (lines/conics), integral points are governed by Pell/congruence conditions — these are the identity families; are there genus-1 plane sections with positive rank for all n? Then infinitely many rational points — but integrality is the catch.
why: Systematises 'plane sections of U_n' as the source of all known identities (genus 0 sections) and asks whether genus-1 sections offer anything (they give rational, not integral, points — usually useless for ES, but integral points on elliptic curves are a finite set with effective bounds, so 'every n has an integral point on some genus-1 section' is at least a well-posed hard problem).
first_step: Classify plane sections of U_n by genus; list which genus-0 sections give Mordell's identities; find a genus-1 section family and compute its rank for small n (Sage) for curiosity.

title: Cubic surface 4xyz = nw(xy+yz+zx) as a Cayley-type nodal cubic: Heath-Brown's Cayley cubic counting
connection: The projective closure is a singular cubic surface. Its singularity type (nodes) places it near Cayley's cubic, whose rational point count was computed by Heath-Brown and de la Bretèche via torsor parametrisations.
why: Universal torsors linearise rational points on singular cubics. An integral-point analogue (torsors over the log pair) could parametrise ES solutions by lattice points in a region.
first_step: Determine the singularity type of the closure (via sympy). If it is a 4A₁ Cayley cubic, write its universal torsor and the integral-points condition in torsor coordinates.

title: Reduction mod p of the ES surface at n = p: counting F_p-points with constraints
connection: U_p mod p degenerates (n ≡ 0) ↔ solutions for 4/p have p | some denominator; the mod-p geometry of the degenerate fibre controls Type I/II.
why: The degenerate fibre xyz = 0 mod p structure is exactly Type I vs Type II split; higher p-adic structure might give Hensel-type existence.
first_step: Write the p-adic Newton polygon / blow-up of U_n at n = 0 and see whether ES(p) is a statement about ℤ_p-points of a model plus a global condition.

title: Transport from multiples: ES(kp) solutions that descend to ES(p)
connection: Solutions for kp do not in general descend to p ↔ but for special k (e.g. k | some denominator pattern), descent works: 4/(kp) = … with k dividing all three denominators ⟹ 4/p.
why: Gives a thick family (all k) of related problems at fixed p; if solutions of 4/(kp) with k | gcd structure are forced for some k, ES(p) follows.
first_step: Compute, for hard p, solutions of 4/(kp) for k ≤ 50 and classify which ones descend; measure descent fraction.

title: Scholz–Brauer addition chains: ∀n statement proved on infinite thin families, open in general
connection: l(2^n − 1) ≤ n − 1 + l(n) is proved for many infinite families and verified computationally, open in general — the same 'thin families proved, no density rung' profile as ES (F30, F23).
why: Compare the family-proof techniques (Brauer chains, Hansen chains) with ES's 3·2^s + 1 family proofs; both rely on algebraic structure of 2^s.
first_step: Read Clift's computational verification and check whether the proved families cover a positive density of n.

title: Mordell's equation for 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 1/w: complete parametrisation of the rational cubic surface
connection: The ES surface is rational; full rational parametrisations (e.g. of Σ1/x_i = 1/w) exist. Integral points of the ES fibre are thin inside the rational points (F13).
why: A parametrisation in which positivity and integrality become linear/congruence conditions could expose the T1 obstruction as a lattice condition and suggest where non-T1 solutions come from.
first_step: Write the standard parametrisation of 1/x+1/y+1/z = 1/w and substitute w = n/4; record the integrality conditions as divisibility conditions.

title: Vieta jumping as a search-space reduction for ES
connection: The Markoff equation and its tree in arXiv:1208.4032 share ES F13/F38/F32: involutions navigate integral solutions, and a decreasing-coordinate argument can yield small certificates.
why: A descent involution is a concrete way to reduce an infinite search to canonical roots. The ES equation (4x−p)yz = px(y+z) is degree 1 in each denominator, so there is no literal Vieta root swap. The available involutions are y↔z and the fibrewise divisor swap d↔p²x²/d on (ay−b)(az−b)=b² with a=4x−p, b=px.
first_step: Write the fixed-x fibre as (ay−b)(az−b)=b² with a=4x−p, b=px. Compose the divisor swap with the coordinate permutations and check integrality and positivity. Then check whether some height decreases outside a finite base set, as in the Markoff tree.

title: Scholz–Brauer: inductive addition-chain constructions
connection: The Scholz conjecture shares F01,F16w,F23,F30: a universal bound is sought, short arithmetic words are certificates, and constructive families establish infinite subcases. ES also has short polynomial certificates and thin proven families.
why: Inductive constructions that append a small chain segment may translate to recursive ES certificate transformations across related n.
first_step: Read the construction for the proved infinite family in the 2023 paper and search for ES maps n↦an+b preserving a unit-fraction certificate.

title: Châtelet surfaces and descent by torsors
connection: Châtelet-type surfaces share F07, F13, F15 and may turn a surface-point question into norm equations and divisor conditions.
why: Descent calculations can uncover a parameterisation more effective than a direct search over three denominators.
first_step: Check whether an ES fibre is birational to a conic bundle with a usable torsor descent; derive the smallest fibre example.

title: U_n's closure is the Cayley 4-nodal cubic σ₃(x,y,z,w)=0 — log CY pair with a triangle through 3 nodes
connection: Substituting w = −4w′/n turns 4xyz = nw(xy+yz+zx) into σ₃(x,y,z,w′) = xyz+w′(xy+yz+zx) = 0, the Cayley cubic (checked: singular exactly at the 4 coordinate points). U_n = Cayley cubic minus the triangle w=0 through three nodes; the Markoff k=4 surface is the same cubic minus a triangle avoiding the nodes.
why: Places ES next to Markoff in the classification of log Calabi–Yau cubic pairs and pins down the one geometric difference (boundary through vs. away from nodes) — any Markoff-type tool must explain what it does at the nodes.
first_step: Write the explicit projective equivalence to x²+y²+z²−xyz = 4 closure and map the U_n boundary triangle and the integral structure (w′ = −n/4) across; record which Markoff automorphisms preserve the ES boundary.
refs: Bright–Loughran, Brauer–Manin obstruction for Erdős–Straus surfaces, Bull. LMS 52 (2020)

title: Harpaz–Wittenberg fibration method along the x-fibration of U_n
connection: HW prove that the Brauer–Manin obstruction is the only one for fibrations over P¹ whose fibres satisfy it, under a fibration hypothesis (proved in many cases); fixing x gives a fibre ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = (nx)², a split torus-like curve whose integral points are divisors of (nx)².
why: Makes precise the sense in which ES is 'a fibration whose fibres are divisor problems' and which hypothesis (Schinzel/HL-type) would be needed.
first_step: State the HW-type conjecture for integral points of this fibration and identify the exact divisor-problem hypothesis it needs at n = p.
refs: Harpaz–Wittenberg, On the fibration method for zero-cycles and rational points, Ann. Math. 183 (2016), arXiv:1409.0993

title: Uniform dimension growth (Castryck–Cluckers–Dittmann–Nguyen) for upper bounds on f(n)
connection: CCDN prove uniform polynomial-in-degree bounds for rational points of bounded height on projective varieties (determinant method); f(n) is a count of integral points of bounded height on U_n.
why: Uniform upper bounds f(n) ≪ n^ε are inputs for second-moment/variance arguments.
first_step: Compare the CCDN bound applied to U_n with the trivial divisor bound f(n) ≪ n^{ε}; see whether it gives anything uniform in a range of heights.

title: Corvaja–Zannier degeneracy of integral points via the subspace theorem
connection: CZ (Annals 2004) prove non-density of integral points on affine surfaces whose boundary has many components; U_n's boundary has 3 lines (log CY), the borderline case where integral points may be dense.
why: Adding extra boundary (e.g. requiring x,y,z to avoid primes in a set S, i.e. S-integral constraints) pushes into the CZ degenerate regime — giving finiteness of 'too-structured' solution families.
first_step: Determine the number of boundary components needed for CZ when imposing 'xyz is S-smooth' and deduce a finiteness lemma for S-smooth ES solutions across n.
refs: Corvaja–Zannier, On integral points on surfaces, Ann. Math. 160 (2004)

title: Universal torsors of the Cayley cubic for parametrising ES solutions
connection: Integral points on singular del Pezzo surfaces are parametrised via universal torsors (Derenthal, Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc); the Type I/II divisor forms are presumably the torsor equations of U_n.
why: A torsor parametrisation makes integral points into lattice points with coprimality — the setting for geometry-of-numbers and circle-method counts.
first_step: Compute the Cox ring of the minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic (blow-up of P² in 6 points of a complete quadrilateral) and write the torsor equation with the ES boundary.

title: Conic bundle over the x-line: Châtelet-surface toolbox (descent, Schinzel's hypothesis)
connection: The x-fibration is a conic bundle with split degenerate fibres. Châtelet surfaces and conic bundles have Hasse principle results conditional on Schinzel's hypothesis (Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc–Swinnerton-Dyer) and unconditional ones in some degrees (Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov).
why: It is the canonical way the field produces points fibrewise. Integral and positivity constraints are what is missing, but the fibration method with additive combinatorics (Green–Tao input) is a powerful modern variant.
first_step: Write the x-fibration's degenerate fibres as linear forms in x. Check whether Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov's linear-forms setting applies to integral points with x in a short range.
refs: Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov, Rational points on pencils of conics and quadrics with many degenerate fibres (Ann. Math. 2014)

title: ES₅ words as integral points of a twisted M₀,₅ (A₂ cluster surface birational to M₀,₅)
connection: The A₂ cluster variety is M₀,₅ (configurations of 5 points on P¹), up to passing to open subsets (the A2 cluster surface is dP5 minus a pentagon of lines, whereas M_{0,5} is dP5 minus all ten boundary lines, so the relationship is birational/open-subset, not equality). Positive integral friezes correspond to special integral points. The coefficient-N pentagon is a twist/deformation. Integral points of M₀,₅ over ℤ[1/S] are governed by S-unit equations.
why: This brings the S-unit equation toolbox (finiteness, effective bounds, counting) and the cross-ratio coordinates of M₀,₅ to ES₅ words.
first_step: Write the five frieze entries as cross-ratios of 5 points on P¹ and identify the N-twist; check whether words correspond to points of M₀,₅ with cross-ratios in a multiplicative set related to N.

title: Square-tiled surfaces with p squares: cylinder decompositions ↔ words
connection: Origamis (square-tiled surfaces) with p squares have cylinder decompositions with heights, widths and twists satisfying Σ h_i w_i = p. A 3-cylinder decomposition with parameters (t,u,v)-type could encode tuv − u − v = p and the sign as a monodromy-group property.
why: Origami monodromy groups (subgroups of S_p) have classifications. 'Monodromy contains an odd permutation' style conditions are Legendre-type (Zolotarev: (A/p) is the sign of x ↦ Ax on ℤ/p).
first_step: Using Zolotarev's lemma, (A/p) = sign of the permutation x ↦ Ax mod p. Look for an origami with p squares whose horizontal/vertical permutations are x ↦ x+1 and x ↦ Ax, and whose cylinder structure encodes the word.

title: Brauer class (tu − 1, p) on the word surface: the ES₅ sign as a Brauer–Manin evaluation
connection: On W_p, the quaternion algebra 𝒜 = (tu − 1, p) defines an Azumaya algebra on the open subset W_p° = {tu ≠ 1}, which contains all positive words; on W_p it is ramified along {tu − 1 = 0} (there u = −p, t = −1/p, and the residue is the non-square class of p), so one must work on W_p° or look for another, unramified class. Its Hilbert symbol at p (local invariant 0 or 1/2) is (tu − 1 / p) = the sign. By the product formula (on W_p°), the sign equals the product of the Hilbert symbols at the other places (2, ∞, q | tu − 1), which is the slot lemma.
why: It would make the slot lemma an instance of Brauer–Manin reciprocity and ES₅ a statement 'some integral point has non-trivial 𝒜-evaluation at p'. This is the integral-points-with-prescribed-Brauer-evaluation problem (studied for Markoff surfaces by Colliot-Thélène–Wei–Xu).
first_step: Confirm the ramification of (tu − 1, p) along tu = 1 and at the boundary of a compactification, and decide whether evaluation on the open set W_p° (a ramified/log Brauer evaluation) is a meaningful obstruction-theoretic statement; compute local evaluation maps at 2 and ∞ and compare with the slot lemma.
refs: Colliot-Thélène–Wei–Xu, Brauer–Manin obstruction for Markoff surfaces (2020; check)

title: Positive proportion of levels with a certificate is false — find the right normalisation
connection: Selberg's positive-proportion step needed the right normalisation (zeros up to height T). For ES at fixed p, only ≍ log²p of ≍ p levels carry certificates; identify the natural finite set of 'attempts' of which a positive proportion succeed (e.g. levels C ≤ (log p)^A, windows e ≤ (log p)^B with weights), so that a positive-proportion statement would be meaningful and imply ES.
why: A positive-proportion statement over a small set of attempts is a pointwise statement; finding the set where proportions are stable is the first step.
first_step: For hard primes, compute success proportions over attempt sets of various shapes and sizes; find shapes where the proportion stays bounded below as p grows.

title: Hecke-orbit world: ES certificates as points in a Hecke orbit on a Shimura curve
connection: If ES solutions at p correspond to CM points or Heegner points on a quaternionic Shimura curve (via the quaternion form of ES), then existence is an equidistribution/non-emptiness of Hecke orbits (Duke, Iwaniec).
why: Equidistribution of Heegner points is proved unconditionally (Duke) for large discriminants, with ineffective Siegel issues; this would make ES ineffectively true for large p if the dictionary is exact.
first_step: Check y1_heegner_level_t.md and QUATERNION_ES.md for whether such a dictionary has been attempted; identify the discriminant attached to p.

title: Spectral world: ES as a statement about eigenvalues of the Laplacian on the triangle orbifold S²(x,y,z)
connection: Area of S²(x,y,z) is 2π(1 − 4/n) for ES triples; Weyl's law relates area to eigenvalue counts, and Selberg trace formula for Δ(x,y,z) involves 1/x, 1/y, 1/z via elliptic terms.
why: Turns the Egyptian equation into a trace-formula identity; spectral rigidity results (isospectrality) could constrain which triples share areas — e.g. how many ES triples exist for given n.
first_step: Low priority; write the elliptic contributions in the trace formula for Δ(x,y,z) and see if 'area = 2π(1 − 4/n)' has a spectral characterization.

title: Vieta moves on lifted equations
connection: Introduce an auxiliary variable making an ES constraint quadratic, then examine Vieta root exchange.
why: Lifting may create useful symmetries absent from the original equation, but integrality must be checked.
first_step: Try y+z=s and yz=q, derive the lifted equations, and test root-exchange closures.

title: Modular congruences for representation counts
connection: Check whether a theta-encoded certificate count has coefficient congruences that force nonvanishing in a useful subsequence.
why: A nonzero residue of an integer count would certify positivity, but the modular-form identification needs verification.
first_step: For a proved quadratic reduction, test coefficient residues modulo a small prime and check the relevant modular-form literature.

title: Theta-quotient expansions as identity catalogs
connection: Inspect explicit q-expansions of a campaign-relevant theta quotient for coefficient identities suggesting arithmetic parametrizations.
why: Formal series relations may point to new exact constructions if the coefficient interpretation is established.
first_step: Derive a short q-expansion from the defining product or sum and check each coefficient interpretation independently.

title: Automorphic periods as counting interpretations
connection: Ask whether an already established lattice or quaternion count can be expressed as a period with arithmetic coefficient meaning.
why: A period formula would connect geometric symmetry to exact counts, but requires a concrete identity rather than analogy alone.
first_step: Write the finite count explicitly and search for an existing period formula matching its group, stabilizer, and congruence level.

title: Gross–Zagier / Waldspurger: the count of certificates as a toric period, nonvanishing ⟺ L(1/2) ≠ 0
connection: If the certificate count is a sum of a theta-type function over a torus orbit (CM points), Waldspurger's formula expresses |sum|² as L(1/2, f × χ) — nonvanishing of L-values implies nonvanishing of the count. Non-vanishing of L(1/2) for *every* twist in a family is open in general, but for specific families (e.g. by Goldfeld's conjecture) it holds for 'most'.
why: Converts ES-like positivity into L-value nonvanishing — a well-studied (if hard) target with GRH-conditional results (one nonvanishing twist among polylog many). Need the dictionary.
first_step: Formulate: is Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} χ(d) (χ of order 2 mod 4C with χ(−1) = −1) a toric period of an Eisenstein series? (Eisenstein, not cuspidal — then Waldspurger is replaced by Hecke's formula for L(s, χ)L(s, χ') — which is explicit!) Compute: the twisted divisor sum Σ_{d|N} χ(d) = coefficient of E(χ,1); positivity of this coefficient at N = 4Cp+1 is the question; it factors over primes q | N as Π (1 + χ(q) + … ); it's zero iff some prime q ∥ N has χ(q) = −1 … so the sign structure is completely explicit per C. Document.

refs: Waldspurger, Sur les valeurs de certaines fonctions L automorphes en leur centre de symétrie, Compositio 54 (1985)

title: Theta series of the ES 'certificate lattice' and its Eisenstein/cusp split
connection: Repo has theta quotients ↔ Siegel–Weil: the Eisenstein part is the genus average; the cusp part is the fluctuation.
why: For ternary forms the cusp part at prime index is bounded by Duke's subconvexity; for ES-type objects identifying the 'weight' and 'level' tells whether subconvexity could ever beat the main term.
first_step: Write R(p) as Fourier coefficient of a (possibly mock / indefinite) theta series; identify weight and level growth.

title: Lattice-point counting in −Γ₁(c) with fixed upper-right entry p (Kloosterman/Kuznetsov for Γ₁(c))
connection: ES₅ ⇔ ∃ c ≥ 2, γ = [[a, p],[c, d]] ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c), a, d in the word range, and (a/p) = −1. So γ ∈ −Γ₁(c)·(unipotent) with fixed b = p. Kuznetsov's formula for Γ₁(c) (with nebentypus) counts such matrices with smooth weights.
why: It gives the precise spectral-theory native form, with the Jacobi twist making it a metaplectic Kuznetsov (Proskurin) problem. B3 says the main term is too small, but the c-sum gives many groups.
first_step: Write the c-summed count as a sum over Γ₁(c) Kloosterman sums S(0, p; c)-type and record the main term size; check with METAPLECTIC_ES.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0088] Formulate R(p) as Σ_{γ ∈ U\Γ/…} with b-entry p and congruence; compute its spectral expansion's main term and check it equals M₀.

title: Weil representation and theta correspondence for the ES quadratic slice
connection: For fixed C, Type II is a binary quadratic condition ↔ Weil representation of SL₂ on Schwartz functions of the quadratic space.
why: Theta correspondence links counts on the orthogonal side to automorphic forms on SL₂ side; might identify R(p) partial sums with Fourier coefficients of explicit Eisenstein series.
first_step: Write the quadratic space (V,Q) for the C-slice and compute its Weil-representation theta function; compare coefficients with slice counts.

title: OAI 178 deterministic nonbipartite Ramanujan graphs (claimed) — explicit expanders for ES search
connection: OAI 178 claims deterministic constructions of Ramanujan graphs of all fixed degrees; explicit expanders give derandomised search/sampling over large certificate spaces.
why: Computational: deterministic sampling of (C,d) certificate grids with guaranteed coverage could make adversarial ES searches (DISPROOF_AVENUES) more efficient.
first_step: Check whether an expander walk over C ∈ [1, X] gives better coverage of ES certificates per factoring call than linear scan on hard primes.

title: Expander walk sampling + Ramanujan graphs for Monte Carlo estimates of M_BM constants
connection: Expander-walk Chernoff bounds give sharp concentration for Monte Carlo with few random bits; estimating Euler-product-type constants and certificate densities by sampling primes benefits.
why: Minor computational gain; listed as a concrete use of Ramanujan-graph technology.
first_step: Implement expander-walk sampling of primes in [X, 2X] and compare variance of estimates of mean f(p) with i.i.d. sampling.
refs: Gillman, A Chernoff bound for random walks on expander graphs, SIAM J. Comput. 27 (1998)

title: Borcherds products / divisors of automorphic forms with zeros at CM points
connection: A Borcherds product has explicit divisor supported on Heegner/CM points. If ES failure at p corresponded to a CM point where some form must vanish, the Borcherds lift might prohibit it.
why: It is the native 'existence via zeros of modular functions' tool, with exact divisor formulas. Speculative but categorically meaningful.
first_step: Read BRAINSTORM/bsC_valence_borcherds.md for the prior attempt; identify which weakly holomorphic input (principal part) would encode certificate data.
refs: Borcherds, Automorphic forms with singularities on Grassmannians (Invent. 1998)

title: Positive entropy from arithmetic recurrence on certificate shapes
connection: Bourgain–Lindenstrauss: Hecke recurrence forces positive entropy, ruling out concentration on small sets. ES: Hecke-like correspondences on certificate shapes (if they exist, cf. LINNIK-ERG item) would force any limiting distribution of shapes to be spread, hence to charge every region with positive mass.
why: Speculative but it is the precise ingredient that made QUE every-form.
first_step: First establish a correspondence (see Hecke-operator item); then measure numerically the entropy of the shape distribution of (★) solutions as p grows.

title: Davenport constant / Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv with a prescribed target
connection: Zero-sum theory gives sequence lengths forcing a subsequence product equal to 1; ES needs a subproduct (with complement structure) equal to −1 — a 'target' variant of Davenport's constant for (ℤ/4C)^×.
why: For small moduli 4C, the group (ℤ/4C)^× is tiny and Davenport-type constants are small — a finite combinatorial lemma might force −1 once N has enough prime factors in the right classes.
first_step: For hard primes, compute Ω((p+e)/4) vs D((ℤ/e)^×) for small e; count e where Ω exceeds the Davenport bound.
